title: Detecting failure: timeouts, heartbeats and gray failure
goal: By the end you can pick a timeout from a measured distribution of delays and say what each side of the trade costs, explain how TCP's retransmission timer, phi accrual and SWIM with Lifeguard adapt to what they see, and recognise a gray failure, where the health check says up while users see errors.

warmup.q: A cluster marks a node dead after 2 seconds without a heartbeat. Heartbeats are sent every second, and the slowest one last week took 1.4 seconds to arrive. Once a day the node stops for a 3-second garbage collection pause. What happens once a day?
options: Nothing: 2 seconds is above the slowest heartbeat ever seen
The cluster declares the node dead during the pause and moves its work, while the node is alive and about to carry on
The heartbeat thread keeps sending during the pause, so nobody notices
The node notices its own pause and tells the cluster it was only slow
warmup.why: A stop-the-world pause stops every thread, the heartbeat thread included, so for 3 seconds the node sends exactly what a dead node sends: nothing. After 2 seconds the cluster can't tell the difference and acts. The node can't warn anyone either, because it doesn't run at all during the pause. The week's slowest heartbeat measures the network, not the node's own pauses.

sections.h: A timeout trades detection time for false alarms
sections.body:
Lesson 1 ended with silence that can mean six things. Every failure detector in production turns that silence into a decision the same way: if nothing has arrived for T milliseconds, suspect the node. **Heartbeats** make the silence measurable: the node sends a small "I'm alive" message every second, so a healthy node is never quiet for long. The only design question left is T, and neither side of it is free.

Make T long and a dead node takes T to notice. If the dead node leads a payments database, writes stall for T plus the failover. Requests routed to it pile up: at 2,000 authorizations a second, a 10-second timeout strands 20,000 of them.

Make T short and you raise **false alarms**: you declare a live node dead because one heartbeat was slow. That costs more than it seems. The "dead" node's work goes to another node while the original may still be doing it, which is lesson 1's duplicate problem with a whole node's worth of work. Its load moves to nodes that may already be busy, their heartbeats slow down, and the next false alarm follows; a cluster can talk itself into declaring everyone dead. Bailis and Kingsbury's survey has a real case: Elasticsearch split into two clusters on about 1 start in 10, because discovery sometimes took longer than its 3-second timeout. Raising it to 15 seconds fixed it.

So you pick T from data. Measure the gaps between heartbeats over days and machines, and put T beyond the gaps you see in normal running. The figure shows the shape you'll find: most gaps sit close to the interval, and a tail runs off to the right. Every gap to the right of T is a false alarm, and every millisecond of T is time a dead node goes unnoticed.

The lab's two links make this concrete. On a calm LAN path, where each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms, the gaps stay within a few milliseconds of 1 second, and a 1.5-second timeout notices a crash in 1.5 seconds with no false alarms in 5 minutes. On a jittery path between regions, 30 to 830 ms per heartbeat, the same timeout fires 15 times in 5 minutes on a node that never failed. A 3-second timeout is quiet on both, and makes the calm link wait twice as long as it needs to. One number can't suit both links, and the next section stops using one number.

try.title: Fixed timeouts on two links
steps: Predict: a 1.5-second timeout on the jittery link, where each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms. How many false alarms in 5 minutes?
Run the demo. It sends a heartbeat every second for 300 s, kills the node, and asks each detector every 10 ms whether it suspects the node. Ignore the phi rows until the next section.
Why does the 3-second timeout take 3,009 ms to notice the crash on the calm link but 3,719 ms on the jittery one?
try.expect:
```text
The node dies at 300 s

calm LAN: each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms               0                   0 ms     1509 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               0                   0 ms     3009 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6009 ms
phi > 8                      0                   0 ms     1569 ms
phi > 12                     0                   0 ms     1709 ms

jittery WAN: each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms              15                1540 ms     2219 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               0                   0 ms     3719 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6719 ms
phi > 8                      0                   0 ms     3449 ms
phi > 12                     0                   0 ms     3889 ms
```

On the jittery link a gap is 1,000 ms plus the difference between two delays, so it can reach 1,800 ms, and 15 gaps in 300 crossed 1.5 seconds. Detection is measured from the crash: the clock starts when the last heartbeat is sent, but the timeout starts when it arrives, so on the jittery link the last heartbeat's own delay (about 700 ms here) is added.

sections.h: Adaptive timeouts learn what normal looks like
sections.body:
TCP met this problem for itself decades ago. Its retransmission timeout, from the networking track's TCP performance lesson, isn't a fixed number. RFC 6298 keeps a smoothed round-trip time and a smoothed variation, and sets the timeout to the smoothed RTT plus four times the variation. Each new measurement moves the average by 1/8 of the difference and the variation by 1/4. A steady path gets a tight timeout and a jumpy path a loose one, and nobody chooses either. (Linux adds a floor of 200 ms.)

The **phi accrual detector** (Hayashibara and colleagues, 2004) applies the same idea to heartbeats, and reports a level of suspicion instead of a yes or no. The Partitioning track's Cassandra lesson showed it in a running cluster: phi is minus the base-10 logarithm of the probability that a healthy node would be this quiet, so phi 1 means one chance in 10 and phi 8 one in 100 million. Cassandra models the gaps with an exponential distribution, which needs only their mean. The original paper, and Akka's cluster, model them with a normal distribution, using the mean and the standard deviation of the last 1,000 gaps. That is the version the lab builds, and the standard deviation is what lets it adapt to jitter.

Work through the numbers. Phi crosses 8 when the silence is about 5.6 standard deviations past the mean gap. On the calm link the gaps barely vary, so the detector's floor of 100 ms on the standard deviation applies, and it suspects after about 1,000 + 5.6 × 100 = 1,561 ms of silence. On the jittery link the gaps' standard deviation is about 330 ms, so it waits about 2,800 ms. Each link gets its own timeout from its own history: phi 8 has no false alarms on either link, and notices a crash in about 1.6 seconds on the calm one and 3.4 on the jittery one.

Now freeze the node for 4 seconds, a long GC pause. Every detector that notices crashes in under 4 seconds suspects the paused node: phi on both links, the 3-second timeout, all of them. That isn't bad tuning. For those 4 seconds a paused node and a dead node send exactly the same thing, nothing, so the only way never to suspect a 4-second pause is never to suspect anything sooner than 4 seconds. There is a second effect: the 4-second gap now sits in the window and raises the standard deviation, so phi takes about 2 seconds instead of 1.6 to notice the next real crash. Cassandra doesn't record gaps longer than 2 seconds for exactly that reason.

A detector only ever suspects. The rest of this track makes sure a wrong suspicion can't corrupt data: fencing tokens in lesson 5, majorities in lesson 7. The detector's job is to make the common case fast.

try.title: A 4-second pause
steps: Run the demo with `pause`: the node freezes for 4 seconds at 199 s, then runs normally until it dies at 300 s.
Which detectors raise exactly one false alarm? Which raise none, and what does that cost them at 300 s?
Compare phi's detection time on the calm link with the run without a pause. Where do the extra 430 ms come from?
try.expect:
```text
The node freezes for 4 s at 199 s, then dies at 300 s

calm LAN: each heartbeat takes 1 to 5 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms               1                2500 ms     1509 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               1                1000 ms     3009 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6009 ms
phi > 8                      1                2440 ms     1999 ms
phi > 12                     1                2300 ms     2239 ms

jittery WAN: each heartbeat takes 30 to 830 ms
detector          false alarms  suspected while alive   detection
fixed 1,500 ms              16                4070 ms     2109 ms
fixed 3,000 ms               1                1030 ms     3609 ms
fixed 6,000 ms               0                   0 ms     6609 ms
phi > 8                      1                1380 ms     3619 ms
phi > 12                     1                 960 ms     4129 ms
```

Every detector faster than 4 seconds raised one false alarm for the pause (the 1.5-second timeout on the jittery link has its 15 jitter alarms on top). Only the 6-second timeout stayed quiet, and it pays 6 seconds for every real crash. Phi on the calm link now needs 1,999 ms instead of 1,569 ms: the 4,001 ms gap is one of the 1,000 in its window and roughly doubles the standard deviation it computes, so the detector stays more patient until that gap ages out of the window.

sections.h: SWIM asks others before it accuses, and Lifeguard asks itself
sections.body:
Heartbeats to one monitor work for a handful of nodes. A cluster where every node watches every other sends n × (n − 1) heartbeats a second: with 1,000 nodes, about a million messages a second to learn that nearly everyone is fine. And each verdict rests on one path: if the link from A to B is the faulty one, A suspects B while everyone else can reach it.

SWIM (Das, Gupta and Motivala, 2002) fixes both, and the Partitioning track's Cassandra lesson sketched it. Each protocol period, every member pings one member chosen at random. If no ack comes back in time, it doesn't accuse yet: it asks k other members to ping the target on its behalf (a ping-req). Only if none of them gets an ack does it mark the target **suspect**. A suspect isn't dead. The suspicion spreads by gossip, riding on the pings members send anyway, and the suspect, when it hears it, refutes it by raising its **incarnation number**, a counter only the member itself may increase. If no refutation comes within the suspicion timeout, the member is declared dead. The expected time to first detection and the messages each member sends stay the same as the cluster grows. HashiCorp's memberlist library, under Consul and Serf, runs SWIM with, in its LAN settings, a probe every second, a 500 ms probe timeout and 3 indirect checks. The stepper walks through one round.

Lifeguard (Dadgar, Phillips and Currey at HashiCorp, 2017) looked at the false alarms SWIM still raised and found that many came from the accuser, not the accused. A member starved of CPU, or paused, misses acks that did arrive, then suspects healthy peers. So each member keeps a local health score that gets worse when its own probes fail or when it has to refute suspicions about itself, and while that score is bad it stretches its probe interval and timeout, by up to 8 times in memberlist. A suspicion's timeout also starts long and shrinks as more independent members confirm it. HashiCorp reported more than 50 times fewer false positives under CPU exhaustion, with no slower detection of real failures.

Cassandra's version of this, from the Partitioning track, is blunter: a node that was itself frozen for more than 5 seconds marks nobody down when it wakes. If you write a monitor of your own, give it the same guard. Check how late the monitor's own loop ran, with `System.nanoTime()` against when it should have run, and skip that round's verdicts when the monitor was the one that wasn't listening.

The suspicion is dropped.</text></svg>
frames.say: B was only paused. When it hears the rumour about itself, it raises its incarnation to 5 and gossips *alive, incarnation 5*. A higher incarnation beats any suspicion about a lower one, so every member drops it.

frames.say: If B really crashed, nobody refutes. When the suspicion timeout ends (it scales with the log of the cluster size in memberlist), B is declared **dead** and the news spreads the same way. Lifeguard makes that timeout start long and shrink as independent members confirm the suspicion.

sections.h: Gray failure: the detector and the user disagree
sections.body:
Every detector so far asks one question: does the node answer? Huang and colleagues at Microsoft (HotOS 2017) found that most of the Azure incidents they studied weren't crashes but **gray failures**: a component that keeps passing its health checks while failing at its real job. Their key term is **differential observability**: the part of the system that suffers (the application, the user) sees the failure, and the part that decides whether to act (the failure detector, the load balancer) doesn't. In one of their cases, a driver bug broke the networking inside some VMs. The VMs kept looking healthy, because their heartbeats went through a host agent over a local channel that didn't use that network, and nothing recovered them until users complained.

Redundancy makes this worse, in a way you can compute. A datacenter network has many equal core switches, and each packet's path crosses one of them. When a switch dies, routing goes around it. When it drops some packets and still answers its own checks, nothing goes around it. With n core switches and a request that fans out to m servers, each over a random path, the chance that the request touches the gray switch is 1 − ((n − 1)/n)^m. One sub-request with 16 switches: 6%. A scatter-gather query with a fan-out of 100: 99.8%. The query is as slow as its slowest part, so one gray switch slows nearly every large request, and more switches means more chances that one of them is gray.

Health checks lie the same way inside your own service. A liveness check that only proves the process answers HTTP stays green while all 20 database connections are stuck behind a lock and every payment times out. The Try shows that case. A deeper check, which borrows a connection and runs `SELECT 1`, catches it, but it has a cost of its own: when the shared database is slow, every instance fails its deep check at the same moment, and a load balancer that removes them all turns a slow database into a full outage. AWS's Builders' Library article on health checks describes load balancers that fail open for this reason: when every instance fails, they send traffic to all of them.

The better fix closes the observability gap: judge health by the requests users send. A synthetic payment that runs the whole path every few seconds sees what a user sees. So does outlier detection in the client or proxy (Envoy has it), which stops sending to an instance whose real requests keep failing, however green its health check is.

try.title: Fan-out and a health check that lies
steps: Predict: with 64 core switches, what share of requests with a fan-out of 100 touch the one gray switch?

Run the demo. Part 1 prints `chanceToTouchGray` for 4, 16 and 64 switches. Part 2 runs a payments service whose 20 database connections are stuck from 20 s to 50 s, checked every second by two kinds of health check.
Which check would have taken the instance out of the load balancer? Which would have done the same to every instance if the database itself were slow?
try.expect:
```text
Chance that one request touches the one gray switch
switches    fan-out 1         10        100      1,000
4               25.0%      94.4%     100.0%     100.0%
16               6.3%      47.6%      99.8%     100.0%
64               1.6%      14.6%      79.3%     100.0%

A payments service, 100 requests a second; all 20 database connections stuck from 20 s to 50 s
seconds        users served   shallow check (live)   deep check (ready)
0-10                   100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
10-20                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
20-30                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
30-40                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
40-50                    0%                 10 of 10                0 of 10
50-60                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
60-70                  100%                 10 of 10               10 of 10
```

With 64 switches and a fan-out of 100, 79% of requests cross the gray one; at a fan-out of 1,000, all of them do. In part 2 the shallow check reports 10 of 10 every window while users get nothing for 30 seconds: that is differential observability in one table. The deep check sees it, and for the same reason it would fail on every instance at once if the database itself were slow.

refs.title: Huang et al.: Gray Failure, the Achilles' heel of cloud-scale systems (HotOS 2017)
AWS Builders' Library: Implementing health checks

analogy: A friend on a long hike promised to text every half hour. An hour passes with nothing. She may have fallen, or be in a valley with no signal, or her phone died, and from your sofa those look the same. You set your deadline from experience: on the mountain route she's often 40 minutes late, on the city walk never, so you wait longer for the mountain (phi). Before you call rescue you ask two friends whether they've heard from her (SWIM's ping-req), and you check that your own phone has signal (Lifeguard). The analogy breaks when the false alarm ends. A hiker who turns up after you called rescue is glad to be found. A node that was declared dead and wakes from a pause carries on with what it was doing, perhaps still believing it leads the cluster, so the rest of the system has to stop it from acting (lesson 5's fencing).
in_your_world: Your Kafka consumers run two detectors, and the pair is a lesson in differential observability. A background thread sends heartbeats to the group coordinator, and `session.timeout.ms` (45 seconds by default since Kafka 3.0) decides when a silent consumer is dead. That thread keeps a consumer alive even if your processing thread is stuck on a slow call, so Kafka added a second check, `max.poll.interval.ms` (5 minutes by default): a consumer that doesn't call `poll` that often leaves the group, even with healthy heartbeats. Kubernetes probes your Quarkus pods the same way: point the liveness probe at `/q/health/live` with checks that only a restart can fix, give it a failure threshold that outlasts your worst GC pause, and put database checks in readiness. Temporal's activity heartbeat timeout is a failure detector for workers: a long settlement activity that heartbeats every 10 seconds can be retried elsewhere soon after its worker dies, instead of waiting for the whole start-to-close timeout.
mistake: The common mistake is pointing a Kubernetes liveness probe at a deep health check, one that queries the database or calls the issuer. The day the database slows down, every pod fails liveness together, kubelet restarts them all, and the restarted pods hit the slow database with cold caches and full connection pools, which slows it further. A slow dependency has become a full outage that restarts can't fix. People do it because a deeper check feels more honest, and in a sense it is: it notices the gray failure. The fix is to split the questions. Liveness asks only "is this process stuck in a way a restart would cure?" and has a timeout longer than your worst GC pause. Readiness may check dependencies, so a pod stops taking traffic without being killed. And the end-to-end view, synthetic payments and error rates per instance, goes to alerts and outlier detection rather than to the restart button.

compare.title: A liveness check and a readiness check in Quarkus

a.label: Shallow: is the process up?
a.title: ProcessUp.kt

b.label: Deep: can it reach the ledger?
b.title: LedgerReachable.kt

compare.note: Both use the MicroProfile Health API that Quarkus serves at `/q/health/live` and `/q/health/ready`. The left one can't see a gray failure in the database path; the right one can, because it needs the same pooled connection a payment needs. That is also its danger: if the ledger database is slow for everyone, every instance goes not-ready together. Put the deep check in readiness, which takes an instance out of rotation without restarting it, never in liveness. (Quarkus registers a datasource readiness check like this one by itself when the health extension and a datasource are present.)

worked.title: Build a phi accrual detector from a fixed timeout

steps.say: Start with a fixed timeout: remember the last heartbeat, suspect when the silence is longer than T. One number for every link.
Record what normal looks like: the gaps between heartbeats, a window of the last 1,000, with running sums so each check costs the same however big the window.
Turn the window into a mean and a standard deviation, with a floor, so a perfectly regular link doesn't make the detector suspect a gap 1 ms longer than usual.
steps.code:
val mean = sum / gaps.size
val variance = max(sumOfSquares / gaps.size - mean * mean, 0.0)
val stdDev = max(sqrt(variance), minStdDevMs)            // 100 ms by default

steps.say: Ask the bell curve how unusual this silence is, and take minus the log. `probabilityLater` is the area to the right of the silence under a normal curve with that mean and deviation.
steps.code:
val p = probabilityLater((nowMs - last).toDouble(), mean, stdDev)
return -log10(p)                                          // 1: one in 10; 8: one in 100 million

steps.say: Check the numbers by hand. Gaps of exactly 1,000 ms, so the 100 ms floor applies. At 1,000 ms of silence p = 0.5 and phi = 0.30. At 1,500 ms the silence is 5 deviations late: p = 2.9 × 10⁻⁷, phi = 6.54. Phi passes 8 at about 1,561 ms, 5.6 deviations late.

lab.title: Fixed timeouts against phi accrual, and the gray switch
steps: Read `Heartbeats.kt` (given): `arrivals` turns a `Scenario` (a link, pauses, a crash) into heartbeat arrival times in virtual time, and `score` asks a detector every 10 ms whether it suspects the node and counts false alarms and detection time. Run the tests from the `labs` folder: all 17 fail.

Exercise 1: `FixedTimeoutDetector`. Suspect only when the silence is strictly longer than the timeout, and never before the first heartbeat. Run `--tests 'sfz.dist.l02.ScenarioTest'`: the fixed-timeout tests pass, including the two jqwik properties about a 4-second pause.

Exercise 2: `PhiAccrualDetector.heartbeat` and `phi`. Keep the last `windowSize` gaps; use the population standard deviation, floored at `minStdDevMs`; return 0.0 until there is a gap. `DetectorTest` checks phi against hand-computed values: 0.30 at the mean, 6.54 at five deviations.
Exercise 3: `chanceToTouchGray`, one line. Then run all 17 and read `ScenarioTest`: it states this lesson's claims as numbers.
hints: `last?.let { nowMs - it > timeoutMs } ?: false` is the whole of `suspects`.
An `ArrayDeque<Long>` with `addLast` and `removeFirst` keeps the window. Computing the mean and variance by looping over 1,000 gaps on every check is fine here; running sums are faster.
Population variance: the mean of the squares minus the square of the mean. Floor it at 0.0 before `sqrt`, because rounding can make it a tiny negative number.
`(1.0 - 1.0 / paths).pow(fanOut)` is the chance that every sub-request misses the gray path.

drill.title: Phi by hand and in code
drill.prompt: From memory, write `phi(nowMs)` given `gaps`, `last` and `minStdDevMs`, calling `probabilityLater(elapsed, mean, stdDev)`. Then, without running anything: gaps have mean 1,000 ms and standard deviation 300 ms. Roughly when does phi pass 8, and why does a fixed 1.5-second timeout misbehave on the same link?

recap: A failure detector turns silence into suspicion with a timeout. Long timeouts notice crashes late; short ones declare live nodes dead, which duplicates work and shifts load until the cluster cascades.
Pick a timeout from measured gaps, or let it adapt: TCP's RTO is the smoothed RTT plus four times its variation, and phi accrual sets suspicion from the mean and spread of recent heartbeat gaps.
While a node is paused it looks exactly like a dead one. Any detector faster than your longest pause will suspect it; correctness must come from fencing and majorities, not from the detector.
SWIM checks before it accuses (ping-req through k members, suspect before dead, refutation by incarnation number) at a constant cost per member; Lifeguard makes a sick accuser slow down.
Gray failure is differential observability: users see the failure and the detector doesn't. With fan-out m over n paths, 1 − ((n − 1)/n)^m of requests touch one gray path.
Health checks lie unless they use the request path. Keep liveness shallow, put dependencies in readiness, and judge health by real or synthetic requests.

quiz.q: From lesson 1: your detector suspects the issuer's node, and the payment service reroutes the in-flight `pay-77` to a standby issuer node. The first node was only paused. What can happen to `pay-77`?
options: Nothing: the detector's suspicion proves the first node never processed it
It is charged twice, unless both issuer nodes check the same idempotency key in shared storage
It is lost, because a suspected node discards its queue
The standby refuses it, because TCP sees a duplicate
quiz.why: A suspicion is not proof: the paused node still holds `pay-77` in its socket buffer and charges it when it wakes. The standby charges it too. The idempotency key from lesson 1 prevents the double charge only if both nodes record keys in the same place, in the same transaction as the charge. TCP can't help: the reroute is a different connection to a different machine.

quiz.q: A phi accrual detector has seen 1,000 gaps with mean 1,000 ms and standard deviation 20 ms, and a floor of 100 ms. Roughly how long a silence makes phi pass 8?
options: About 1,110 ms
About 1,560 ms
About 8,000 ms
About 18,400 ms
quiz.why: The floor replaces the measured 20 ms with 100 ms, and phi 8 is about 5.6 deviations past the mean: 1,000 + 5.6 × 100 ≈ 1,560 ms. Without the floor it would be about 1,110 ms, which would turn every small hiccup on a quiet LAN into a false alarm. 18,400 ms is Cassandra's exponential model with a 1-second mean, which ignores the spread entirely.

quiz.q: In SWIM, member A gets no ack from B and none of A's three ping-req helpers gets one either. B is alive but was paused for 3 seconds. What stops the cluster from declaring B dead?
options: A waits for a second probe period before suspecting
B is first only suspected; when it wakes and hears the suspicion, it raises its incarnation number and gossips that it's alive, which overrides the suspicion
The helpers' acks arrive later and cancel the suspicion
Nothing: SWIM declares B dead as soon as the indirect probes fail
quiz.why: SWIM separates suspect from dead. During the suspicion timeout, B can refute with a higher incarnation number, a counter only B may raise, and every member prefers the higher incarnation. Late acks to an old probe don't cancel anything, and SWIM doesn't wait for another period before suspecting.

quiz.q: A search request fans out to 200 shards across 32 equal core switches. One switch drops 5% of packets but answers its own pings. About what share of search requests touch it?
options: About 3%
About 5%
About 50%
About 100%
quiz.why: 1 − (31/32)^200 ≈ 1 − e^(−6.3) ≈ 0.998. Each sub-request has a 1-in-32 chance, but with 200 of them nearly every request has at least one on the gray switch, and the request is only as fast as its slowest sub-request. 3% is the chance for one sub-request, and 5% is the switch's own loss rate.

quiz.q: A payment service's liveness probe calls a check that runs `SELECT 1` on the ledger database with a 2-second timeout. One evening the database slows to 3-second queries. What happens?
options: Nothing: liveness only matters at start-up
Every pod fails liveness at about the same time and Kubernetes restarts all of them, adding cold starts and reconnect storms to a slow database
Only the pods with slow connections are restarted, which fixes them
The pods are taken out of the load balancer but keep running
quiz.why: A deep check measures a shared dependency, so all pods fail it together, and liveness failure means restart. Restarts can't make the database faster and add load to it. The last option describes a readiness failure, which is where a dependency check belongs, and even there all pods leaving at once needs the fail-open behaviour from the AWS article.

flashcards.front: What does a short failure-detection timeout cost?
flashcards.back: False alarms: live nodes declared dead, their work duplicated and their load shifted onto other nodes, which can cascade.

flashcards.front: How does TCP set its retransmission timeout (RFC 6298)?
flashcards.back: Smoothed RTT plus four times the smoothed RTT variation, updated with weights 1/8 and 1/4 per sample; Linux floors it at 200 ms.
A healthy node would stay this quiet with probability 10⁻⁸, judged from the recent heartbeat gaps. With a normal model, about 5.6 standard deviations past the mean gap.

flashcards.front: Why can no detector tell a 4-second pause from a crash in under 4 seconds?
flashcards.back: Both send nothing during that time. Only waiting longer than the pause separates them.

Ping a random member; if no ack, ask k others to ping it (ping-req); if still nothing, mark it suspect and gossip that. It refutes with a higher incarnation number, or is declared dead after the suspicion timeout.
The component that suffers from a failure (the app, the user) sees it, while the one that detects and reacts (health checks, load balancer) doesn't. The mark of a gray failure.

flashcards.front: Liveness or readiness for a database check?
flashcards.back: Readiness: it takes the pod out of rotation without restarting it. Liveness should only catch what a restart cures.

terms.plain: A small periodic message that says only "I'm alive", so silence becomes measurable.
A detector suspecting a node that is alive, slow or paused.
A detector that outputs a suspicion level from how unusual the current silence is, given recent heartbeat gaps.
A gossip membership protocol: random probes, indirect probes through k members, suspicion before death, refutation by incarnation number.
A counter only a member may raise about itself, used to override older suspicions.
A component that passes its health checks while failing at its real work.
The failure is visible to the users of a component but not to whatever monitors it.

explain_back.prompt: Your team wants to cut the failover timeout of the payments database's leader from 10 seconds to 1 second, because "failover should be fast". Explain what that changes and what you would measure first.
explain_back.answer: A timeout doesn't detect crashes, it detects silence, and a leader is silent during a GC pause, a VM hiccup or a slow network as well as after a crash. At 10 seconds we pay up to 10 seconds of stalled writes per real crash. At 1 second we'd notice crashes faster but also declare the leader dead every time it pauses or a packet queue spikes for a second, and each false failover is risky: a new leader is elected while the old one may wake up and keep accepting writes until it's fenced, and the extra failovers move load at the worst moment. So before choosing, I'd measure the heartbeat gaps and the leader's own pauses over a few weeks, including the tail, and put the timeout past the longest pause we're willing to treat as normal. Better still, use an adaptive detector like phi accrual, which waits longer on a jittery link and less on a calm one. And whatever we choose, correctness shouldn't depend on it: the old leader must be fenced with an epoch or token, so a wrong suspicion costs time, not data.

deeper.body:
**Fail-slow hardware.** Gray failure has a hardware cousin. Gunawi and colleagues' "Fail-Slow at Scale" (FAST 2018) collected 101 reports, from 12 institutions, of disks, SSDs, CPUs, memory and network parts that kept working far below their normal speed, and of the long cascades they set off in clusters that only knew "up" and "down". TigerBeetle's fault model lists a disk that becomes very slow without returning an error as one of the faults its tests inject.

**The accrual idea in other places.** Akka's cluster uses the normal-distribution phi detector with a threshold of 8 and adds an *acceptable heartbeat pause* to the mean, a budget for GC pauses it shouldn't suspect. Its documentation suggests a threshold of 12 in clouds with more jitter. Cassandra's exponential variant ignores the spread and depends only on the mean gap, which is simpler and more patient on calm links.

**Detectors in theory.** Chandra and Toueg (1996) classified failure detectors by how wrong they may be, for example "eventually every crashed node is suspected, and eventually some correct node is never suspected", and showed which kinds are enough to solve consensus. Lesson 7 of this track and the Consistency and consensus track use that result: consensus protocols stay safe with an unreliable detector and only need it to be right eventually to make progress.

*Designing Data-Intensive Applications*, 2nd edition, chapter 9, discusses timeouts and the limping-node problem with further references.
